newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian TV advertising spend seen doubling by 1998.
newsitem.headline: Indian TV advertising spend seen doubling by 1998.

text.p: Indian television advertising is expected to touch 20 billion rupees in 1998 from around 10 billion rupees in 1995, the president of an advertising agency said on Friday.
"TV spending was around 1,000 crores (10 billion rupees) in 1995," Raj Gupta, president of Karishma Advertising, a subsidiary of advertising multinational Lintas India, said.
"It's expected to touch 2,000 crores by 1998," he added.

Gupta was speaking to reporters at a news conference to launch Unitas Television Corporation, a joint venture of Lintas India and Indian television serials maker United Television (UTV). UTV is 30 percent owned by film studio 20th Century Fox.
Gupta is the chief executive designate of the new firm.
Prem Mehta, Lintas' chief executive officer and Ronnie Screwvala, chairman of UTV, said the new firm will fuse the advertising skills of Lintas and the programming skills of UTV.
Unitas will have a starting capital of 10 million rupees.
"This is the first venture of its kind ... that will cultivate brand relevant audiences through television software development," the two firms said in a joint statement.
Gupta said the new firm would attempt to produce information and entertainment programmes that would match the customer profile targeted by the advertiser.
Both producers of soaps and office automation products target today's popular televison serials, Gupta said.
"You wouldn't advertise cement in the Readers' Digest," Gupta said, saying the print media offered a more focused audience.
He said Unitas would evaluate the performance of programmes against pre-set goals and change new episodes of a programme to ensure the relevant audience viewed it.
"Our intention is to go as far as how many who buy branded shirts watched my programme," said Prem Mehta, Lintas India CEO.
Gupta said research tools were now available to dissect viewership to find out viewers' age, income status and mental outlook -- whether they were conservative or modern.
"Is it something like advertising dictating editorial content in some newspapers?" asked a journalist.
Gupta said no. He said the question is "Is my ad seen by the maximum number of the right people with minimum wastage." If the programme did not entertain, no one would see it, he said.
"We are not tampering with the medium, only adding on," said Screwvala. He promised sharper and more entertaining programmes.
